This is an Insight article, written by a selected contributor as part of GIR's co-published content. Learn more about Insight

The term “artificial intelligence” was first coined in 1955.[1] Even prior to this, there were several key events that shaped the thinking that underpins “AI” (eg, in 1950, Alan Turing introduced the “imitation game” to assess whether a machine could exhibit human-like intelligent behaviour).[2] In recent years, however, AI has advanced rapidly in development, accessibility and use, particularly generative artificial intelligence (GenAI).

Legal practitioners and investigators have always had to keep pace with and adapt to various technological advancements in conducting or responding to investigations. Accordingly, the need to adapt to technology is not a novel challenge. However, the relative ease of access to GenAI tools and their integration into systems used by firms, investigative agencies, regulators, legal practitioners and the judiciary, requires a step change to (1) realise the benefits and efficiency gains of appropriately deploying AI tools and (2) manage the associated challenges and risks. Some of these challenges and risks are novel but some are existing risks that are exacerbated.

This chapter assesses (1) the impact of AI across different phases of an investigation, (2) the focus on AI-assisted investigation methods by regulators and agencies, (3) confidentiality and privilege issues posed by the use of AI and (4) potential harms from the use of AI in the context of investigations. We focus largely on developments in the United Kingdom but these will be of interest to firms and advisers across the world.

There is no universally accepted definition of AI.[3] Across the world, many governments, regulators, organisations, industry bodies and think-tanks have attempted to tailor the definition of AI depending on the specific context and purpose. These definitions have also gone through several iterations (eg, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) updated its previous definition in 2023).

From a global perspective, the OECD definition of AI has influenced domestic legislation and policy. The OECD has defined an AI system as:

a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Different AI systems vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment.[4]

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act adopts a definition that is materially the same as the OECD definition.[5]

The UK government has defined AI with reference to two characteristics: “adaptivity” and “autonomy”.[6] These features are broadly consistent with the approach taken by the OECD and the European Union. In our view, the simplest definition from a legal perspective has been provided by the UK Jurisdiction Taskforce, which defines AI as “a technology that is autonomous”.[7] This definition is technology-agnostic and it determines that the key novel characteristic of AI is autonomy.[8]

Similar to the definition of AI, there are many ways to categorise AI. In this chapter, the primary focus is on the impact of GenAI as opposed to traditional and predictive AI tools.

Traditional AI, including predictive and conversational AI, has long been used in investigations to automate repetitive tasks, promote consistency and optimise processes. These tools rely on predefined rules and algorithms to run workflows, analyse data and trends, and generate forecasts or predictions (eg, predictive coding or technology-assisted review (TAR), which uses machine learning to extrapolate document-review results from a small manually reviewed “seed set”).[9]

GenAI uses deep learning algorithms to generate new outputs based on large quantities of existing or artificially created input data. The outputs of these systems tend to mimic human-like responses. The Law Society of England and Wales (The Law Society) notes: “In simple terms, traditional AI recognises, while GenAI creates.”[10]

Agentic AI refers to systems that can be programmed to autonomously make decisions and perform tasks with limited or no human supervision or intervention (eg, virtual assistants).[11] The key difference between agentic AI and GenAI is that agentic AI has the “ability to accept goals and autonomously sequence and execute multi-step actions across systems rather than only producing single prompt and then response outputs as produced by [GenAI]”.[12]

While there has been a significant increase in the application of GenAI tools by lawyers, it appears that there is relatively little use of agentic AI tools in legal practice according to The Law Society.[13] This is likely to change as agentic AI tools develop.

GenAI tools provide an opportunity to create significant efficiency gains and cost savings when conducting internal investigations or responding to authority-led or regulator-led investigations. This opportunity needs to be counterbalanced with the potential risks of using AI (eg, potential loss of confidentiality or privilege depending on how and which GenAI tools are used and potential AI harms owing to risk of hallucinations).

Although GenAI tools can be usefully deployed, appropriate oversight for the use of AI in such investigations is of paramount importance to ensure that the risks are adequately mitigated.

Corporate investigations can differ significantly depending on the circumstances of each case. The factors that may arise include potential monetary exposure, reputational sensitivity, complexity, reporting risks, the likelihood of potential external investigations or litigation and cross-border risks. These factors will determine (1) the type of AI tools that are appropriate, (2) which phases of the investigation merit the use of AI and (3) the level of human oversight required to appropriately navigate the use of AI.

For individuals under investigation, there may be different considerations at play depending on whether they have legal representation. There is considerable evidence of litigants-in-person placing heavy reliance on public GenAI tools. There are potential confidentiality and privilege issues to consider in such scenarios (discussed below in the section titled “Legal professional privilege and AI”).

At the issue detection, or triaging, stage, many firms and corporates use AI to (1) monitor and detect red flags and (2) consider the merits of complaints. This in turn informs the assessment of whether further investigation is required or reporting obligations are triggered. The advantage of utilising AI to provide speedy and reliable triaging outcomes cannot be underestimated, especially given the large volume of complaints and enquiries.

Although there is a risk that some of these investigative steps may not be covered by legal professional privilege, that risk is not novel to AI. It can exist at the issue detection stage (even without the use of AI) as enquiries often arise from the business directly or via compliance or risk functions and are not always conducted by in-house or external lawyers.

If a matter has been identified as requiring further investigation, depending on the significance, scale and sensitivity of the matter, an assessment should be made as to whether in-house or external lawyers should conduct the investigation and if such an investigation would benefit from the use of AI tools.

In this investigation phase, GenAI provides a significantly faster option compared with a traditional eDiscovery review and may lead to an improvement in accuracy in comparison with traditional TAR,[14] which has been used for over a decade.
